rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The low starting organic fraction preserves early retention, and the strong endpoint reduces the risk of missing late compounds.

Injection 1 already reached the maximum CRF of 1.000. Shorten the gradient while holding temperature and endpoints fixed to seek a faster fully resolved method and measure the critical pair’s slope response.
The 8-minute gradient retains full resolution with a minimum R of 3.24. Shorten by another grid step to reduce analysis time while testing whether the early critical pair remains above R = 1.5.

Shorten the gradient another step while keeping selectivity conditions fixed. The observed slope response suggests the early critical pair may still meet R = 1.5, yielding an even faster method at the maximum CRF.

Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary. The early pair will likely fall below R = 1.5; retain injection 4 as the fastest fully resolved method while assessing whether temperature optimization could make this shorter gradient viable.

Test whether higher temperature improves the early critical pair’s selectivity enough to rescue the 2-minute gradient. Holding the gradient fixed isolates the temperature response; injection 4 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Heating reduced resolution, so test the lowest temperature with the same 2-minute gradient. This will establish whether cooling restores sufficient selectivity or whether a shallower gradient is needed.

Narrow the gradient span at the temperature that gave the best early-pair selectivity. The shallower slope should raise its resolution above 1.5, while the final hold will test whether the last compound still elutes quickly enough to retain maximum CRF.

Shift the successful 0.70-wide gradient window upward, preserving its slope while strengthening the final hold to accelerate the last peak. This tests whether the early pair retains sufficient resolution with a higher starting organic fraction.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten the fastest fully resolved method further. The shallower gradient may improve separation, but the early pair must be checked for compression as it approaches the unretained region.

Increase temperature one step to shorten retention while testing the early pair’s remaining resolution margin. Keep the gradient fixed, since larger temperature increases previously reduced selectivity.

Raise phi0 one step to test whether a narrower gradient can shorten the run while preserving full resolution. Monitor the early pair closely because its first peak is already near the unretained region; injection 11 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Return phi0 to 0.30 and test the next temperature step to establish the thermal limit of the fastest fully resolved method. The early pair may drop below R = 1.5; if so, injection 11 remains the preferred speed-optimized method.

Reduce the gradient span to recover early-pair resolution at 35 C without increasing gradient duration. The stronger retention during the final hold may modestly delay the last peak, but should leave ample margin below the 10-minute scoring threshold.

Lower phi0 to retain the early pair beyond the gradient-delay region, where the shallower gradient can better separate it. Injection 14 showed that reducing slope alone barely helped this pair at phi0 = 0.30; this tests recovery of full resolution at 35 C.

Reduce phi1 one grid step to make the gradient shallower with the early pair still retained. Its R of 1.42 is close to the threshold, so this change may recover maximum CRF while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Refine around injection 11, the fastest confirmed fully resolved method, by lowering phi1 one step to seek additional resolution margin with minimal extra retention. Injection 16 is borderline despite its rounded CRF of 1.000, so retain injection 11 as the preferred method.

Shift injection 11’s gradient window down by 0.05 while preserving its slope, testing whether better early retention maintains full resolution away from the unretained region. The endpoint remains strong enough to keep the last peak well below the time-penalty threshold.

Lower phi1 one step from injection 18 to increase the early pair’s narrow resolution margin while maintaining useful initial retention. This should provide another maximum-CRF method with greater separation margin, though injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed option.

Cool injection 17 by one step to increase the critical pair’s resolution margin while retaining a short run. This explores a less borderline maximum-CRF alternative; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Lower phi0 one step from injection 20 to keep the first peak farther from the unretained region while preserving the favorable low-temperature selectivity. This should provide a fully resolved, short-run alternative with more resolution margin than injection 18.

Test a lower starting organic fraction with the strongest endpoint to improve early retention without extending the final hold. The early pair may retain sufficient resolution at 25 C, offering a fast maximum-CRF alternative farther from the unretained region.

Lower phi1 one step from injection 22 to improve its borderline early-pair resolution while preserving stronger initial retention. This should retain maximum CRF with only a modest increase in last-peak time; injection 11 remains the fastest confirmed method.
